senses: Having power to enact or establish as a law.
That which saturates.
A person who supports or believes in segregation.
examples: In 2003, Biden eulogized South Carolina Republican Sen. Strom Thurmond, one of the most notorious segregationists in American politics for most of his career who had “moved to the good side” later in life, Biden said.
On March 18, 1965, Wallace, who was a segregationist, told the Alabama legislature that he intended to ask for federal troops “to provide for the safety and welfare of the so called demonstrators.”

senses: Staying intact in the stomach, then dissolving in the intestine.
ety: From Ancient Greek ἐντερικός (enterikós, “intestinal”). By surface analysis, entero- + -ic.

senses: A French delicatessen.
A musical organ, consisting of steam whistles played with a keyboard. Often used with merry-go-rounds.
ety: From Ancient Greek Καλλιόπη (Kalliópē, “Calliope, the muse of poetry”), from καλός (kalós, “beautiful”) + ὄψ (óps, “voice”).

senses: To go out, to set forth, to set out.
ety: The noun is derived from modern English out- (prefix meaning ‘away from; toward the outside of’) + go. Sense 1 (“cost, expenditure, or outlay”) was probably modelled on income. Cognates * Scots outgae * West Frisian útgean * Dutch uitgaan * German Low German utgahn * German ausgehen * Swedish utgå

senses: To add an endcap to.
Having a balustrade.
The bark of the root of this plant, used for medicinal and (mostly historically) culinary purposes and formerly a main ingredient in root beer.
ety: From Spanish sasafrás, possibly from Latin saxifragus (“stone-breaking”) from the habit of certain plants growing in cracks in boulders. If this etymology is correct, it is a doublet of saxifrage.

senses: A Provençal dish consisting of puréed or finely chopped olives, capers, anchovies, and olive oil, usually eaten with bread as an hors d'œuvre.
ety: Borrowed from French tapenade, from Provençal and Occitan tapenada, tapenado, a diminutive of tapeno (“caper”), variant of tàpero, from Old Occitan tapera, from Latin capparis (“caper”). Influenced by Old Occitan tapia (“rammed earth”), referring to caper bushes growing against buildings made of rammed earth.

senses: Of an organism, having characteristics of a single sex (as opposed to hermaphrodites).
Unisex; suitable for any sex or gender.
examples: You may not be familiar with the name or it could be a unisexual name, and some women and men may have first names that are more traditional for the opposite gender.

senses: To attend an event as a spectator; to observe.
Below an apex.
Capable of being assumed, or taken to be true.
Capable of being assumed, or taken on.
Of a mortgage: such that a subsequent homebuyer can take on the existing balance, interest rate, and other terms.
That inhibits the growth and reproduction of fungi but does not kill off their population.
ety: International scientific vocabulary, from New Latin, from fungi- + -static = fungistasis + -ic.

senses: A type of round, white turnip from Japan.
examples: Many foods that seem exotic for New England are turning up in small amounts at more and more farms: kohlrabi, hakurei turnips, okra, edamame, Jerusalem artichokes, ground cherries and quince.

senses: capable of being decided.
A supporter of natalism; one who is in favour of childbearing.
A sacred grove in ancient Celtic religion.
ety: Borrowed from Gaulish νεμητον (nemēton), from Proto-Celtic *nemetom.

senses: The part of the foot between the toes and the ankle, especially its five bones.
One who compromises; especially, one who compromises readily
examples: The word on Ken Salazar, tapped by President-elect Barack Obama to run the Interior Department, is that he is friendly, approachable, a good listener, a genial compromiser and a skillful broker of deals.

senses: One who flings or hurls something.
The presence of two close or overlapping statements of the subject of a fugue, especially towards the end.
An acceleration in the tempo of an opera that produces an ending climax.
ety: Borrowed from Italian stretto. Doublet of strait and strict.

senses: A player of war games.
Someone who demurs.
A flip-flop (type of footwear)
ety: Blend of Japanese + sandal, originally a genericized trademark.

senses: The loose skin at the back of the neck of some animals.
ety: 1790, from earlier (1787) scuft and dialect scuff, influenced by scruff (“crust”). Related to North Frisian skuft (“back of the neck of a horse”) and Dutch schoft (“withers (of a horse)”), from Proto-Germanic. Compare also Old Norse skopt (“hair of the head”), Gothic 𐍃𐌺𐌿𐍆𐍄 (skuft, “hair of the head”), Middle High German schopf (German Schopf).

senses: A small tube, often with an enlargement or bulb in the middle, and usually graduated, used for transferring or delivering measured quantities of a liquid.
The quality of being drivable, of being easy or pleasant to drive
examples: Challenges included the engine's high internal temperatures, its thirstiness in low-speed operation and the need to improve drivability for operators accustomed to V-8 power.

senses: The system of seven tones built on a tonic key; the 24 major and minor scales.
A sound of specific pitch and quality; timbre.
The quality of all the tones in a composition heard in relation to the tonic.
The interrelation of the tones in a painting.
A button allowing the user to subscribe to an RSS feed.
ety: From Chiclets, a brand of chewing gum pieces which the buttons resemble, from chicle + -let.

senses: Imitating; copying; not original.
Modelled after another thing.
Chosen for the sake of its effect, rather than for its own sake; sometimes distinguished from real.
ety: From Ancient Greek μεθοδικός (methodikós, “going to work by rule, systematic, crafty”).

senses: The process of removing the magnetic field from an object.
ety: From de- + magnetization or from demagnetize + -ation.

senses: Someone or something that starches.
Any American marsupial of the family Didelphidae in the order Didelphimorphia.
ety: From Powhatan aposoum (“white animal”), from Proto-Algonquian *wa·p-aʔθemwa (“white dog”); compare Ojibwe waabasim (“white dog”).

senses: Medicine used in deworming an animal.
Without nuts (the fruit).
Without the use of nuts (the mechanical fastener).
The Japanese red pine, Pinus densiflora.
